title: Luke 15:11–32
context: The third parable tells of a father and two sons. The younger son demands his inheritance, wastes it, and, starving, comes to his senses and returns home, hoping to be a servant. His father runs to meet him, embraces him, and throws a feast. The elder son, angry at the celebration, refuses to go in, and the father comes out to plead with him too. The story ends open: will the elder brother join the feast? Both traditions read it as a portrait of the Father’s grace toward both the openly rebellious and the self-righteous. Their main difference is how they read the son “coming to himself.”

verses.text: He said, “A certain man had two sons.
verses.arminianNotes: “A certain man had two sons.” From the start, both sons matter to the story. Arminian readers note that the parable is aimed at the grumblers of verse 2 as much as at sinners.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Both traditions see the elder son as an essential part of the parable, not an afterthought.

verses.text: The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me my share of your property.’ So he divided his livelihood between them.
verses.arminianNotes: The younger son demands his share early, which in that culture would have been deeply shameful. The father grants it. Arminian readers stress that the father lets the son go, respecting his freedom even when it is misused.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a picture of sin’s rebellion against the Father. Both traditions agree the father’s patience is remarkable.

verses.text: Not many days after, the younger son gathered all of this together and traveled into a far country. There he wasted his property with riotous living.
verses.arminianNotes: The son travels far away and wastes everything in reckless living. Arminian readers note that sin brings real loss.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers make the same point. Both traditions see the “far country” as life away from God.

verses.text: When he had spent all of it, there arose a severe famine in that country, and he began to be in need.
verses.arminianNotes: A famine strikes, and he starts to go hungry. Arminian readers see consequences that God can use to awaken a sinner.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providence at work in the hard circumstances. Both traditions note that suffering often prepares the way for repentance.

verses.text: He went and joined himself to one of the citizens of that country, and he sent him into his fields to feed pigs.
verses.arminianNotes: He hires himself out to feed pigs, unclean animals for a Jew. Arminian readers note how low he has fallen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same. This verse is shared ground.

verses.text: He wanted to fill his belly with the pods that the pigs ate, but no one gave him any.
verses.arminianNotes: He longs to eat the pigs’ pods, but no one gives him anything. Arminian readers note the emptiness of what the world offers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same, reading it as a picture of the sinner’s helpless state. Both traditions find the depth of his need painfully clear.

verses.text: But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough to spare, and I’m dying with hunger!
verses.arminianNotes: “When he came to himself” marks the turning point. He remembers his father’s generosity. Arminian readers often see this as a genuine response to grace: prevenient grace awakening the sinner, who then truly chooses to turn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the parable is not a full account of how conversion works, and that Scripture elsewhere teaches that God gives the new heart that makes such a turn possible. Both traditions agree the turn is real, and both caution against building a complete doctrine on one parable.
verses.keyContrast: Both see real repentance here. Arminians commonly see the son responding freely to prevenient grace; Reformed readers commonly hold that such coming to oneself flows from God’s prior, effectual work, though the parable does not describe it.

verses.text: I will get up and go to my father, and will tell him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight.
verses.arminianNotes: He plans to go back and confess, “I have sinned against heaven and in your sight.” Arminian readers note that true repentance includes honest confession.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same. Both traditions treat his confession as a model of repentance.

verses.text: I am no more worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: He feels unworthy to be a son and plans to ask to be a hired servant. Arminian readers note that he still thinks he must earn his way back.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers make the same point, contrasting his plan with the father’s grace. Both traditions see that grace will exceed his hopes.

verses.text: “He arose and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.
verses.arminianNotes: While he is still far off, the father sees him, is moved with compassion, runs, embraces, and kisses him. An older man running was undignified in that culture. Arminian readers stress the father’s eagerness to receive a returning child.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the father acts first in the meeting, welcoming before the speech is finished. Both traditions see this verse as one of Scripture’s clearest pictures of the Father’s love.

verses.text: The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
verses.arminianNotes: The son begins his confession, but he does not get to the request to be a servant. Arminian readers note that the father’s welcome interrupts the plan to earn a place.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers make the same point: grace ends the bargaining. Both traditions find the omission meaningful.

verses.text: “But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring out the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet.
verses.arminianNotes: The father calls for the best robe, a ring, and sandals, signs of full restoration as a son, not a servant. Arminian readers stress complete reinstatement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often see a picture of justification and adoption, the son clothed in what he did not earn. Both traditions read these gifts as signs of sonship restored.

verses.text: Bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let’s eat and celebrate;
verses.arminianNotes: He calls for the fattened calf and a feast. Arminian readers note that the celebration is public and generous.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same. Both traditions see the feast as an echo of heaven’s joy (vv. 7, 10).

verses.text: for this, my son, was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found.’ Then they began to celebrate.
verses.arminianNotes: “This, my son, was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found.” Arminian readers often note that the son was alive before leaving, so the language describes a real departure and real restoration, a theme some apply to backsliding.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often hear the language of spiritual death and new life (Ephesians 2:1–5). Both traditions agree the main point is the father’s joy at recovery, and they caution against pressing every detail.

verses.text: “Now his elder son was in the field. As he came near to the house, he heard music and dancing.
verses.arminianNotes: The elder son, coming in from the field, hears the music. Arminian readers note the shift in the story to the second son.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same. This verse is shared narrative ground.

verses.text: He called one of the servants to him and asked what was going on.
verses.arminianNotes: He asks a servant what is happening. Arminian readers note that he does not go straight in to his father.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same distance. This verse is shared ground.

verses.text: He said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and healthy.’
verses.arminianNotes: The servant explains that the brother is home and the father has killed the fattened calf. Arminian readers note the simple, joyful report.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same. This verse is shared ground.

verses.text: But he was angry and would not go in. Therefore his father came out and begged him.
verses.arminianNotes: He is angry and refuses to go in, so the father comes out and pleads with him. Arminian readers stress that the father’s love seeks both sons, and that grace can be refused.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the same pleading love, and see in the elder son the danger of self-righteousness. Both traditions note that the father goes out to each son.

verses.text: But he answered his father, ‘Behold, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a commandment of yours, but you never gave me a goat, that I might celebrate with my friends.
verses.arminianNotes: He complains of years of service and obedience without a feast. Arminian readers note that he relates to his father like a servant, not a son.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see self-righteousness that misses grace. Both traditions see the Pharisees and scribes of verse 2 reflected in him.

verses.text: But when this your son came, who has devoured your living with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him.’
verses.arminianNotes: He calls his brother “this your son” and accuses him of wasting money on prostitutes. Arminian readers note his refusal to claim his brother.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same bitterness. Both traditions see a warning against resenting grace given to others.

verses.text: “He said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.
verses.arminianNotes: The father answers tenderly: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.” Arminian readers stress that the elder son has always had access to the father’s love.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers make the same point: he lived near grace without enjoying it. Both traditions find this gentle reply striking.

verses.text: But it was appropriate to celebrate and be glad, for this, your brother, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: It was right to celebrate, because “this, your brother” was dead and is alive. The parable ends without telling us if the elder son went in. Arminian readers see an open invitation to the hearers to respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the open ending as a challenge to the self-righteous. Both traditions agree that the story invites the listener to join the Father’s joy.
